notes.trap: For DECIMAL input the result is DECIMAL with precision and scale each widened by 4, not DOUBLE, so extra trailing zeros appear. Integer input returns DOUBLE.
notes.example_sql: SELECT avg(col) FROM VALUES (1.0), (2.0) AS tab(col)

notes.trap: `count(a, b)` with several arguments counts only rows where every argument is non-NULL, so one NULL column drops the whole row. `count(DISTINCT a, b)` behaves the same way.
notes.example_sql: SELECT count(a, b) FROM VALUES (1, NULL), (2, 3) AS tab(a, b)

notes.trap: Rows where the predicate evaluates to NULL are not counted; only TRUE counts. The argument must be BOOLEAN, so pass a comparison rather than a number.
notes.example_sql: SELECT count_if(col > 1) FROM VALUES (NULL), (1), (2) AS tab(col)

notes.trap: NULLs are ignored rather than following three-valued AND logic. If every input is NULL, or there are no rows, the result is NULL, not true.
notes.example_sql: SELECT bool_and(col) FROM VALUES (CAST(NULL AS BOOLEAN)), (CAST(NULL AS BOOLEAN)) AS tab(col)

notes.trap: Same as `bool_and(...)`: NULL inputs are skipped, so a group containing true and NULL returns true rather than NULL.
notes.example_sql: SELECT every(col) FROM VALUES (true), (CAST(NULL AS BOOLEAN)) AS tab(col)

notes.trap: Over zero rows, or only NULLs, the result is NULL, not false. `any(...)` and `some(...)` are aliases with identical NULL behaviour.
notes.example_sql: SELECT bool_or(col) FROM VALUES (true) AS tab(col) WHERE col = false

notes.trap: By default NULLs are not skipped, so a NULL row can be returned even when non-NULL values exist. Pass true as the second argument to ignore NULLs.
notes.example_sql: SELECT any_value(col) FROM VALUES (NULL), (5), (20) AS tab(col)

notes.trap: NULL values are silently dropped from the result array. Element order follows row order and is not guaranteed after a shuffle.
notes.example_sql: SELECT size(collect_list(col)) FROM VALUES (1), (NULL), (2) AS tab(col)

notes.trap: NULLs are dropped and element order is unspecified. Wrap the result in `array_sort(...)` if you need a stable order.
notes.example_sql: SELECT size(collect_set(col)) FROM VALUES (1), (1), (NULL) AS tab(col)

notes.trap: This is an alias of `collect_list(...)`: NULLs are dropped, duplicates are kept, and order is not guaranteed.
notes.example_sql: SELECT size(array_agg(col)) FROM VALUES (1), (NULL), (1) AS tab(col)

notes.trap: It returns an actual value from the data, with the input's type, and never interpolates. `percentile(...)` does interpolate, so the two disagree on even-sized inputs.
notes.example_sql: SELECT approx_percentile(col, 0.5) FROM VALUES (1), (2), (3), (4) AS tab(col)

notes.trap: With only one input pair Spark 3.x returns NULL, not NaN. NaN comes back only with spark.sql.legacy.statisticalAggregate=true.
notes.example_sql: SELECT corr(c1, c2) FROM VALUES (1, 2) AS tab(c1, c2)

notes.trap: The sample covariance of a single pair is NULL by default (it was NaN in older versions), whereas `covar_pop(...)` returns 0.0 for the same input.
notes.example_sql: SELECT covar_samp(c1, c2) FROM VALUES (1, 2) AS tab(c1, c2)
